Learning outcomes · today

By the end of this session you should be able to

1

Apply the Galerkin weighted residual method and integration by parts to obtain [k]{T̂}ᵀ = {q} + {b} and explain what each term means.

2

Evaluate the conductance matrix [k] and the load vectors {q} and {b} of a 4-node rectangular element in closed form.

3

Assemble element matrices into the global system with a connectivity table and impose Dirichlet conditions by row–column elimination.

4

Solve a small problem by hand, post-process temperature and flux at a point, and judge the result against a refined mesh.

Check

All four outcomes are examined by Assignment 4 (released today) and by the final exam under CLO3.

Block 1 · 0:00 – 0:30

From residual to weak form

Substitute T = {N}{T̂}ᵀ into the PDE, weight the residual with {N}ᵀ, integrate by parts. Text §2.2.2.

SEAA 4243 · 2D Heat Transfer — Part 2

5

Block 1 · substitute the approximation · text (2.34)

Substituting the approximation leaves a residual

(2.34)

Count

Four unknowns T̂1…T̂4, but only one equation — and it holds nowhere exactly.

Idea

Make the residual zero on average, weighted by each shape function: four weights, four equations.

(2.35) Galerkin: weights = shape functions

Why

Galerkin: the weights are the shape functions themselves, which makes [k] symmetric.

SEAA 4243 · 2D Heat Transfer — Part 2

6

Block 1 · integration by parts: the 1D case you know

Move one derivative from T onto the weight; a boundary term appears

bar element, earlier in the course

Purpose 1 · relax continuity

After IBP only first derivatives of N and T appear, so a piecewise-linear (or bilinear) T is admissible. Second derivatives of a bilinear field would be zero or undefined at element edges.

Purpose 2 · expose the natural condition

The boundary term contains k dT/dx, the flux. Where the flux is specified it becomes a load; where it is zero it vanishes; where T is specified the term is removed with the equation.

SEAA 4243 · 2D Heat Transfer — Part 2

7

Block 1 · integration by parts in two dimensions · text (2.36)

Green’s theorem turns the area integral of a derivative into a boundary integral

Green’s theorem, x-direction (same for y)

(2.36)

Why

nx, ny are the outward normal components and ds runs around the element boundary. Apply it to each row of {∂}[E]{∂}ᵀ.

Watch out

qb = k ∂T/∂n is the boundary flux of (2.15), positive when heat enters. Text (2.41) writes the components with the opposite sign — use (2.15).

Conductance matrix, heat-generation vector, boundary-flux vector

(2.37)

(2.15)

(2.42)

Why

Read [k]’s integrand left to right: {N}ᵀ{∂} means the derivative acts on the weight {N}ᵀ (moved there by the IBP). {∂}ᵀ{N} is the last session’s 2 × 4 gradient matrix.

Block 2 · the whole matrix · text (2.49)

Four distinct values; symmetric; every row sums to zero

(2.49)

Check

Row sums are zero because a uniform temperature produces no flux: [k]{1} = {0}. Use it as a check on every hand calculation.

Watch out

[k] is singular on its own (one zero eigenvalue). Only the Dirichlet conditions make the system solvable.

Uniform generation splits equally; a uniform edge flux splits between the two edge nodes

(2.39)

(2.40)

Why

{b} is assembled only on the elements whose edge lies on the flux boundary; interior edges never contribute.

Check

Dimensions with unit thickness: qhab/4 is W m⁻³ × m² = W per metre of thickness; qbb/2 likewise.

SEAA 4243 · 2D Heat Transfer — Part 2

24

Block 4 · the scatter-add rule

Each local entry is added to the global position that the connectivity table names

In words

  • Start with [K] = 0 (9 × 9) and {R} = 0 (9 × 1).
  • For each element: read its row of the table; add kij to KIJ and ri to RI.
  • Shared nodes receive contributions from every element that touches them.

Why ‘add’

Each element’s weighted-residual equations are statements about its own area; the equation for a global node sums the statements of all elements around it — heat balance at that node.

Check

Assembled [K] is symmetric, sparse (zeros where nodes are not connected) and still singular until Dirichlet conditions are imposed.

Block 4 · impose the known temperatures

Known T: delete the equation, move the value right

Row–column elimination (T̄ = 0)

  • Known: T1 = T4 = T7 = T8 = T9 = 0 (top and left edges).
  • Delete rows and columns 1, 4, 7, 8, 9 of [K] and rows of {R}.
  • Keep rows and columns 2, 3, 5, 6: a 4 × 4 system.

Non-zero T̄ (e.g. 100 K in Assignment 4)

The known column times T̄ is a known heat flow; it moves to the right-hand side before the row and column are deleted. MATLAB: F = F − K(:,dof_k)*To.

(2.54) → (2.55)

Activity 5 · solution

Row 1 closes to within rounding; the pattern of the answer matches the physics

Hottest at node 3

Farthest from the two cold edges, enclosed by the two insulated edges: the prediction from Heat Transfer Part 1 is confirmed.

T₂ = T₆

Symmetry about the diagonal through nodes 1, 5, 9: swapping x and y maps the problem onto itself, so the solution must be symmetric too.

Use symmetry in exams

If a problem is symmetric, equal temperatures are equal unknowns: fewer equations to solve by hand.

Block 5 · temperature at any point: three steps

Find the element, go local, interpolate with its own nodal values

1

Locate the element that contains the point (from the mesh geometry).

2

Local coordinates: subtract the coordinates of that element’s node 1.

3

Interpolate with the shape functions and the element’s four nodal temperatures, in local order.

Watch out

Nodal values in the element’s local order (1)…(4) = its connectivity row, not global order.

SEAA 4243 · 2D Heat Transfer — Part 2

34

Block 5 · flux at a point

Differentiate the same interpolation; the flux is constant along one direction in each element

Reading the sign

At the centroid of element 2 (nodes 2, 3, 6, 5): qx < 0, heat flows towards −x, from the hot corner at node 3 towards node 2; qy > 0, towards the cold top edge.

Discontinuity

The flux jumps across element edges because the gradient of a bilinear field is not continuous. Software averages nodal fluxes; the size of the jump is a free error indicator.

SEAA 4243 · 2D Heat Transfer — Part 2

41

Block 6 · the script, traced against the pipeline

Left: input and [k]. Right: assembly, Dirichlet, solve

% ---- input (text §2.3.1) ----

L = 1; H = 1; kx = 300; ky = 300; Q = 600;

To = 0; % Dirichlet value

Nx = 2; Ny = 2; ndof = 9;

a = L/Nx; b = H/Ny;

 

% ---- local conductance matrix: (2.49) ----

s1 = b*kx/(3*a) + a*ky/(3*b);

s2 = -b*kx/(3*a) + a*ky/(6*b);

s3 = -b*kx/(6*a) - a*ky/(6*b);

s4 = b*kx/(6*a) - a*ky/(3*b);

k = [s1 s2 s3 s4; s2 s1 s4 s3; s3 s4 s1 s2; s4 s3 s2 s1];

fQ = a*b*Q/4*[1; 1; 1; 1]; % (2.39)

% ---- assembly by connectivity ----

K = zeros(ndof); F = zeros(ndof,1);

e1 = [1 2 5 4]; K(e1,e1) = K(e1,e1) + k;

e2 = [2 3 6 5]; K(e2,e2) = K(e2,e2) + k;

e3 = [4 5 8 7]; K(e3,e3) = K(e3,e3) + k;

e4 = [5 6 9 8]; K(e4,e4) = K(e4,e4) + k;

F(e1) = F(e1) + fQ; % ... and e2, e3, e4

 

% ---- Dirichlet: row-column elimination ----

T = zeros(ndof,1);

dof_k = [1 4 7 8 9]; T(dof_k) = To;

F = F - K(:,dof_k)*T(dof_k); % known -> RHS

dof_u = setdiff(1:ndof, dof_k);

T(dof_u) = K(dof_u,dof_u) \ F(dof_u); % solve

Run it: T(dof_u) returns 0.4821, 0.6214, 0.3857, 0.4821 — equation (2.55). Change Nx = Ny = 16 and generalise the assembly loop to reproduce the 16 × 16 column of the table.

Same pipeline, two unknowns per node

Today in four lines

  • Galerkin + IBP: [k]{T̂}ᵀ = {q} + {b}; the operator acts on the weight to its left.
  • [k] from four closed-form values s1…s4; rows sum to zero; {q} = qhab/4; edge flux splits qbb/2.
  • Assembly = scatter-add by connectivity; Dirichlet = move known values right, delete rows and columns.
  • Post-process in local coordinates; refine the mesh before you believe a number.
